newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong newspaper headlines-May 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong newspaper headlines-May 21.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- MING PAO -- Judge and Executive Councillor Andrew Li was nominated by post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa as the first Chief Justice of the Court of Final Appeal after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1. The nomination was welcomed by the government and the legal sector.
-- SING TAO DAILY -- China has decided to disband the Preparatory Committee after its last meeting on July 1, at which President Jiang Zemin will endorse the committee's work and contributions.
-- WEN WEI PO -- At the first anniversary of President Li Teng-hui's term in office, research showed Taiwanese people were unhappy with his work in the past year.

-- TA KUNG PAO -- The first lot of Chinese approved to emigrate to Hong Kong under a new priority points system was announced. The new method was welcomed by the public for its high level of transparency.

-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- Senior government officials were gradually becoming involved in the operation of the post-handover government. Secretary for policy coordination Michael Suen and Immigration Director Regina Ip were going to Beijing on Wednesday to hold meetings with officials of China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs over visa-free entry for foreigners.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- The mania for red-chip listings reached new heights on Tuesday as potential investors snapped up more than 400,000 application forms for shares in Beijing Enterprises Holdings, owned by the Beijing municipal government, on the first day of its public offer.
-- U.S. car giant General Motors Corp was believed to be close to sealing a deal to buy Peugeot Citroen's stake in a money-losing car manufacturing joint venture in Guangzhou.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Individuals or small investor groups might soon be prevented from taking the lion's share of new issues in the first step by regulators to tackle growing concerns about the strain on the money supply.
